pos: v. (present participle; composing, framing in words; literally, bubbling up)
etymology: From Old French enditer, to dictate or compose, from Latin indicere, to proclaim. The margin of older Bibles gives the Hebrew sense as boileth or bubbleth up, the heart overflowing with its theme.
biblical_def: Psalm 45 is a royal wedding song that the New Testament reads as a song of Christ and His bride. It opens with the singer's heart overflowing: “My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue is the pen of a ready writer.” The Hebrew pictures a heart bubbling over like a pot on the fire, so full of its subject that it cannot keep silent. And the subject is the King. The psalm goes on, “Thou art fairer than the children of men: grace is poured into thy lips” (Psalm 45:2), and then addresses the King as God: “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever” (45:6), words that Hebrews 1:8 applies directly to the Son. The inditing heart is therefore a model for all true praise and preaching. The best words about Christ do not come from a cold or calculating mind but from a heart warmed by meditation on His beauty, so that the tongue becomes the ready pen of what the heart has seen. Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh (Matthew 12:34).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): INDITE, to compose; to write; to commit to words in writing; to direct or dictate what is to be uttered or written.
webster_full: INDITE, v.t. To compose; to write; to commit to words in writing.
To direct or dictate what is to be uttered or written.

Psa 45:2

Heb 1:8

corruption_summary: Worship and preaching are reduced to technique and performance, words produced without a heart that has first been filled with the beauty of Christ the King.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word has simply passed out of common use.

What needs recovering is the order the psalm assumes: the heart first, then the tongue. Much modern worship is crafted for effect, and much preaching is assembled from technique, but the psalmist's pen was ready because his heart was full of the King. Meditation on Christ precedes every faithful word about Him.

pos: v.t. (to swear falsely; to break an oath)
etymology: From Old English forswerian, from for-, implying wrongness or negation, and swerian, to swear. To forswear oneself is to swear what is false or to fail to keep what was sworn.
biblical_def: In the Sermon on the Mount the Lord cites the old teaching: “Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths.” The law did forbid swearing falsely by the name of God (Leviticus 19:12) and required that vows be kept (Numbers 30:2). But the scribes had built a casuistry of oaths, teaching that an oath by heaven or by the temple was less binding than one by God's name or by the gold of the temple (Matthew 23:16-22). Christ sweeps the evasion away: “But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil” (Matthew 5:37). Every word is spoken before God, so there is no category of speech in which falsehood is permitted. The Reformed churches have rightly understood this not as forbidding all lawful oaths, for God Himself swore by Himself (Hebrews 6:13) and Paul called God to witness (2 Corinthians 1:23), but as forbidding rash, frivolous and false swearing (1689 Confession, 23.2). The disciple's plain word must be as binding as any oath.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FORSWEAR, to reject or renounce upon oath; to deny upon oath. To forswear oneself, to swear falsely; to perjure oneself.
webster_full: FORSWEAR, v.t. To reject or renounce upon oath.
To deny upon oath.

FORSWEAR, v.i. To swear falsely; to commit perjury.

corruption_summary: Truthfulness is graded by context, so that only sworn statements are thought to bind, while ordinary promises, contracts and marriage vows are broken without shame.
corruption_paragraphs: The Pharisees' scale of oaths has its modern form in a culture that distinguishes the binding statement under oath from the ordinary word that may be bent. Marketing exaggerations, broken contracts and abandoned marriage vows are excused as long as no court is involved.

Christ allows no such scale. Every word is spoken in the presence of God, and the disciple's yea must be yea. Lawful oaths remain a solemn act of worship, but the plain word of a Christian should need no oath to be trusted.

pos: v.t. (to warn beforehand; to caution in advance)
etymology: From fore-, before, and warn, from Old English warnian, to take heed or give notice. The word occurs twice in the Authorized Version, as forewarn and forewarned.
biblical_def: Speaking to His disciples amid the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, the Lord said: “But I will forewarn you whom ye shall fear: Fear him, which after he hath killed hath power to cast into hell; yea, I say unto you, Fear him.” Men can kill the body and after that have no more that they can do (Luke 12:4); God has power over body and soul forever. The warning is given beforehand, while there is still time to heed it, and it is itself an act of mercy. Christ then turns at once to comfort: not one sparrow is forgotten before God, and the very hairs of His disciples' heads are numbered (12:6-7). The fear of God and the comfort of God belong together. Paul uses the word in the same spirit when he writes to the Thessalonians that no man should defraud his brother, “because that the Lord is the avenger of all such, as we also have forewarned you and testified” (1 Thessalonians 4:6). Faithful ministers forewarn because they love; the preacher who will not speak of hell has not loved his hearers as Christ did.

corruption_summary: Preaching that forewarns of hell is dismissed as fear-mongering, and the fear of God is replaced with a God who need not be feared at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Much modern preaching has dropped the warning Christ Himself gave. Hell is reinterpreted as annihilation, as a state of mind, or as a doctrine too harsh for modern ears. The fear of God is redefined as mere respect, and preachers who forewarn are accused of manipulating their hearers.

Christ forewarned because He loved. The same sermon that tells disciples to fear Him who can cast into hell tells them they are of more value than many sparrows. Faithful preaching keeps both, and the 1689 Confession confesses the eternal torment of the wicked (32.2) as the truth from which the gospel offers refuge.

pos: v.t. (to think out or plan beforehand)
etymology: From Latin praemeditari, to consider beforehand, from prae, before, and meditari, to ponder. The Greek promeletao means to practise or rehearse a speech in advance.
biblical_def: Christ foretold that His disciples would be delivered up to councils, beaten in synagogues, and brought before rulers and kings for His sake. He then gave them this promise: “But when they shall lead you, and deliver you up, take no thought beforehand what ye shall speak, neither do ye premeditate: but whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye: for it is not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost.” The command is not a licence for unprepared preaching. It is a word of comfort to persecuted witnesses: they need not lie awake rehearsing their defence, because the Spirit of God would give them what to say. The Acts of the Apostles shows the promise kept, as Peter, filled with the Holy Ghost, answered the Sanhedrin (Acts 4:8), and Stephen's adversaries “were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake” (Acts 6:10). The text also reminds the church that the boldness of martyrs is a gift and not a technique. Ordinary preaching calls for study (2 Timothy 2:15); the hour of trial calls for trust.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PREMEDITATE, to think on and revolve in the mind beforehand; to contrive and design previously.
webster_full: PREMEDITATE, v.t. To think on and revolve in the mind beforehand; to contrive and design previously.
PREMEDITATE, v.i. To think, consider, or revolve in the mind beforehand; to deliberate; to have formed in the mind by previous meditation.

The Holy Ghost would give them what to speak in that hour.

corruption_summary: The verse is misused to excuse unprepared preaching and to claim new, Spirit-given utterances, when it is a promise of help to persecuted witnesses on trial.
corruption_paragraphs: Some preachers cite Mark 13:11 to justify neglecting study, as though the Spirit rewards those who stand up without preparation. Charismatic movements have gone further, treating unpremeditated speech as fresh revelation. Both misread the setting, which is the courtroom of persecution, not the ordinary pulpit.

Scripture commands ministers to study, to give attendance to reading, and to rightly divide the word of truth. The promise of Mark 13:11 is a pastoral gift to the suffering church: when believers stand before hostile powers for Christ's sake, they need not fear, because the Spirit will not leave them without a witness.

pos: v.t. (to count over again; to call to mind and muster)
etymology: From Old French reconter, to tell again or count again, from re-, again, and conter, to count or tell, from Latin computare. In Nahum the Hebrew means to remember or call to mind.
biblical_def: Nahum's prophecy describes the fall of Nineveh, the proud capital of Assyria. As the attackers storm the city, the king of Nineveh musters his nobles: “He shall recount his worthies: they shall stumble in their walk; they shall make haste to the wall thereof, and the defence shall be prepared.” The king calls his mighty men to mind and sends them to the wall, but they stumble as they go. The defence is prepared too late. All the strength of the empire that had carried Israel captive and threatened Jerusalem cannot save the city when the LORD has determined its judgment. “Behold, I am against thee, saith the LORD of hosts” (Nahum 2:13). Nineveh had once repented at the preaching of Jonah, and God had spared it; but a later generation returned to violence and pride, and this time the sentence was executed. To recount one's worthies, to call the roll of one's own strength, is the instinct of every proud power in the day of trouble. Nahum shows how empty that roll is when God is against it, and how sure is the refuge of those who trust Him: “The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble” (Nahum 1:7).

webster_full: RECOUNT, v.t. To relate in detail; to recite; to tell or narrate the particulars; to rehearse.
To count again (in this sense commonly written re-count).

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word survives in ordinary use.

Nations and churches alike are tempted in the day of trouble to recount their worthies, their resources, institutions, numbers and influence. Nahum's word stands: the strength of Nineveh stumbled on the way to the wall. The only strong hold in the day of trouble is the LORD, who knoweth them that trust in Him.

etymology: From feigned, from Old French feindre, to pretend, from Latin fingere, to form or fashion. The Hebrew word means in falsehood.
biblical_def: Jeremiah compares the two sisters, Israel and Judah. Israel, the northern kingdom, had committed adultery with idols and been put away into captivity. Judah saw it and did not fear. Worse, under Josiah's reforms Judah made a show of return: “And yet for all this her treacherous sister Judah hath not turned unto me with her whole heart, but feignedly, saith the LORD.” The temple was cleansed, the passover kept, the idols broken outwardly, but the heart of the people did not follow. The LORD then pronounces a startling verdict: “The backsliding Israel hath justified herself more than treacherous Judah” (Jeremiah 3:11). Pretended repentance is in one sense worse than open rebellion, because it adds hypocrisy to sin and mocks God with outward forms. True repentance is turning with the whole heart, and God promises: “And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart” (Jeremiah 29:13). The 1689 Confession describes repentance unto life as a grieving for and hating of sin, and a turning from it all unto God (15.2), which no outward reform can counterfeit.

webster_full: FEIGN, v.t. To invent or imagine; to make a show of; to pretend; to assume a false appearance.

corruption_summary: Repentance is reduced to outward profession, a raised hand, a prayer said or a reform adopted, without the whole-hearted turning from sin that Scripture requires.
corruption_paragraphs: Revivalist methods and easy-believism have often counted a decision, a walked aisle or a repeated prayer as conversion, and churches have counted reforms of programme as reforms of heart. Judah under Josiah shows how hollow outward return can be.

Scripture demands the whole heart. Repentance unto life is an evangelical grace by which a sinner, seeing the filthiness of his sin and apprehending God's mercy in Christ, grieves for it, hates it and turns from it to God. Anything less is feigned, however orthodox its forms.

etymology: From un-, not, and advisedly, from Old French aviser, to consider, from Latin ad, to, and visum, seen. The Hebrew means to speak rashly or thoughtlessly.
biblical_def: Psalm 106 recounts Israel's rebellions in the wilderness, including the waters of Meribah: “Because they provoked his spirit, so that he spake unadvisedly with his lips.” Moses, the meekest man upon the earth, was provoked by the people's murmuring into rash words: “Hear now, ye rebels; must we fetch you water out of this rock?” (Numbers 20:10). He struck the rock twice instead of speaking to it as commanded, and the LORD said that he had not believed Him, to sanctify Him in the eyes of Israel; therefore he would not bring the congregation into the land (Numbers 20:12). The psalm notes that the people's sin was the provocation, but Moses was held responsible for his own lips. Rash speech in a moment of anger cost the great prophet the promised land. James draws the lesson for every believer: “If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man's religion is vain” (James 1:26). Leaders especially must guard their lips, because they speak for God before His people.

webster_full: UNADVISED, a. Not prudent; not discreet; done without due consideration; rash.
UNADVISEDLY, adv. Imprudently; indiscreetly; rashly; without due consideration.
Psalm 106:33 says Moses spake unadvisedly with his lips at Meribah.
The people provoked his spirit, but he was answerable for his words.
His rash speech and act kept him from entering Canaan (Numbers 20:12).

Jas 1:26

corruption_summary: Rash, angry speech is excused as authenticity or as the natural result of provocation, when Scripture holds every man answerable for the words of his own lips.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern culture prizes unfiltered expression, and provocation is accepted as an excuse for harsh words: they made me say it. Social media rewards the quick, angry reply. Psalm 106 refuses the excuse. The people provoked Moses, and yet the rash words were his and the penalty was his.

Scripture calls believers to be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath (James 1:19). Leaders in the church above all must bridle their tongues, because they speak in God's name and their rash words can misrepresent Him before His people.

pos: n. pl. (lines of descent; family registers)
etymology: From Anglo-French pe de grue, crane's foot, from the three-branched mark used in old genealogical charts to show lines of descent. The Hebrew word means to declare one's birth or descent.
biblical_def: At Sinai, in the second year after the exodus, Moses and Aaron numbered the men of war: “And they assembled all the congregation together on the first day of the second month, and they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names, from twenty years old and upward, by their polls.” Every Israelite had a place, a tribe and a father's house. The registers were not idle curiosity: they established inheritance in the land, membership in the congregation, and, for the priests, the right to serve at the altar. After the exile, men who could not find their register were put from the priesthood as polluted (Ezra 2:62). The pedigrees of Israel were preserved by providence until they had done their work, for they lead to the genealogies of Matthew 1 and Luke 3, which show Jesus to be the Son of David and the Son of Adam. Once Christ came, Paul warned against endless genealogies (1 Timothy 1:4), because a believer's standing no longer rests on descent from Abraham according to the flesh but on union with Christ by faith (Galatians 3:29).

corruption_summary: Two distortions meet here: an obsession with ancestry as identity, and a dismissal of the biblical genealogies as unhistorical lists; both miss their purpose in bringing forth Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Historical-critical scholarship has long treated Israel's genealogies and censuses as late fictions or inflated numbers. Popular culture, meanwhile, has made ancestry a source of identity and pride. Scripture rejects both: the registers are historical records preserved by God, and they serve a purpose beyond themselves.

That purpose was fulfilled in Christ, the promised Seed of Abraham and Son of David. Now the believer's pedigree is in Him: if ye be Christ's, then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise. Pride in descent, whether Jewish or Gentile, has no place in the church.

etymology: From Greek poietes, a maker, from poiein, to make, through Latin poeta. Paul uses the very Greek word in Acts 17:28.
biblical_def: Standing on Mars' hill before the philosophers of Athens, Paul proclaimed the Creator God whom they worshipped as unknown. He said: “For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.” The line “we are also his offspring” comes from the Greek poet Aratus, and a similar phrase is found in Cleanthes. Paul did not endorse the pagan theology of those poets, whose god was Zeus; he took a true fragment of natural knowledge, that man is dependent on and derived from God, and turned it against their idolatry: “Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device” (Acts 17:29). From there he called them to repentance in view of the judgment by the Man whom God raised from the dead. Paul shows that the light of nature leaves men without excuse (Romans 1:20), and that even their own poets testify against their idols. But natural knowledge is not saving knowledge; only the proclamation of the risen Christ calls men to repentance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): POET, the author of a poem; the inventor or maker of a metrical composition; one skilled in making poetry.
webster_full: POET, n. The author of a poem; the inventor or maker of a metrical composition.

Paul turns the pagan line against idolatry (Acts 17:29).

corruption_summary: Paul's quotation is stretched into an endorsement of other religions as paths to God, when he used the pagan poet to convict idolatry and call for repentance before the risen Judge.
corruption_paragraphs: Religious pluralism reads Acts 17 as Paul affirming the truth in all religions and building bridges of common spirituality. But Paul's spirit was stirred in him when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry (Acts 17:16), and his sermon ends with a command to repent and a warning of judgment.

Reformed theology distinguishes the knowledge of God given in nature, which leaves men inexcusable, from the saving knowledge given only in the gospel. Paul used a pagan poet as a witness against paganism, not as a partner in it. Christian apologetics may do the same, but must end where Paul ended: with the resurrection of Christ and the call to repent.

pos: v. (present participle; thrusting oneself in without right)
etymology: From Latin intrudere, to thrust in, from in, into, and trudere, to thrust. Paul's Greek embateuo means to step into or to investigate, possibly a term used of initiation into mystery rites.
biblical_def: The Colossian church was threatened by a teaching that mixed Jewish ceremonies, ascetic rules and visionary mysticism. Paul warned: “Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind.” The false teachers claimed special access to the unseen world through visions, and they paraded a self-imposed humility that refused to come directly to God. But their humility was really pride, for they were puffed up, and their visions were a trespass into what God had not revealed. Their deepest error was “not holding the Head” (Colossians 2:19): they sought spiritual fulness somewhere other than Christ, “in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (2:3). The secret things belong unto the LORD our God, but those things which are revealed belong to us and to our children (Deuteronomy 29:29). Every claim to private revelation beyond Scripture is an intrusion into things not seen, and every religion that adds mediators to Christ beguiles believers of their reward.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): INTRUDE, to thrust oneself in; to come or go in without invitation, permission or welcome; to enter where one has no right.
webster_full: INTRUDE, v.i. To thrust oneself in; to come or go in without invitation, permission or welcome.
To encroach; to enter or force oneself in without permission; to enter uncalled or unwelcome.
INTRUDING, ppr. Entering without invitation or right.
Colossians 2:18 warns against those intruding into things they have not seen.
The false teachers joined worship of angels to a self-made humility.

corruption_summary: Claims of private visions, angelic encounters and extra-biblical revelation are welcomed as deeper spirituality, which is exactly the intrusion into unseen things Paul condemned.
corruption_paragraphs: From medieval mystics and the cult of angels and saints to modern charismatic claims of heavenly visits and fresh words from God, the church has repeatedly been tempted to look past Christ for spiritual experience. Such teaching is often wrapped in humility, yet it exalts the visionary above the ordinary believer who has only the Word.

Paul calls it intrusion into things not seen and the fruit of a fleshly mind. The canon is closed, Christ is the one Mediator, and the sufficiency of Scripture means the believer needs no secret knowledge beyond what God has revealed. Holding fast the Head is the whole of true spirituality.
